claim: The upstream predicted-latency-routing guide's 'Standalone Mode' deploys the llm-d Router with an Envoy sidecar via a Helm chart with no Kubernetes Gateway object, but the entire installation path (kubectl, Helm, Gateway API CRDs, Secrets) is still Kubernetes-native -- 'standalone' means 'no Gateway API object', not 'no Kubernetes'.
stance_target: the term 'Standalone Mode' in llm-d documentation implies a non-Kubernetes deployment path
scope_conditions: llm-d/llm-d guides/predicted-latency-routing README, current as of Sep 9 2026
quoted_support: This deploys the llm-d Router with an Envoy sidecar, it doesn't set up a Kubernetes Gateway. helm install ${GUIDE_NAME} ${ROUTER_STANDALONE_CHART} ...

claim: Across every backend variant documented (GPU/vLLM, TPU, P/D-disaggregated, multimodal, Intel XPU), the guide states the latency predictor is 'EPP-side only, so the model server needs no predictor-specific changes.'
stance_target: predicted-latency scheduling does not require modifying or instrumenting the backend/model-server, only the EPP/router side
quoted_support: Reuse the agentic-serving guide's model server. It is re-labeled llm-d.ai/guide=optimized-baseline so the router values above select it with no changes (same as the GPU path), and the latency predictor is EPP-side only, so the model server needs no predictor-specific changes.

claim: SLO-aware and P/D-disaggregated predicted-latency configurations require streamingMode:true and every client request to be sent with stream:true, because TPOT training samples derive from the inter-token gaps of a streamed response.
stance_target: client-protocol constraint imposed by predicted-latency scheduling in TPOT-prediction configurations
quoted_support: The P/D values file sets streamingMode: true, so clients must send "stream": true. TPOT training samples come from the inter-token gaps of a streamed response, and decode here is scheduled purely on predicted TPOT -- so non-streaming traffic leaves the half of the predictor that places decode with nothing to learn from.

claim: OpenShift support for the predicted-latency-routing guide is currently unreliable as-is, because the latency-predictor sidecars may require additional OpenShift-specific runtime adjustments beyond the shipped manifests; GKE or CoreWeave are the recommended tested platforms.
stance_target: platform-specific caveat for anyone adopting predicted-latency scheduling on a non-vanilla Kubernetes distribution
quoted_support: OpenShift support for this guide is currently not reliable as-is. The latency-predictor sidecars used by predicted-latency scheduling may require additional OpenShift-specific runtime adjustments beyond the manifests in this guide. Until that is resolved, prefer GKE or CoreWeave for the tested path.

claim: Deployment/benchmarking tooling for this guide (llmdbenchmark CLI) auto-deploys a Kubernetes harness pod (llmdbench-harness-launcher) into the target namespace, an additional Kubernetes-coupled dependency in the reference workflow beyond the router itself.
stance_target: even the tooling around llm-d guides, not just the router, assumes Kubernetes
quoted_support: When orchestrating benchmarks via llmdbenchmark, the CLI automatically and transparently deploys a harness pod (llmdbench-harness-launcher) into your namespace.
